The author argues that Constantine’s strategic foresight in establishing Constantinople proved vital as the Huns displaced the Goths [PDF p. 61]. After crushing the Ostrogoths, the Huns forced the Visigoths to seek refuge across the Danube in 376 [PDF p. 62]. The Eastern Emperor Valens, described by the author as stupid and cowardly, permitted their entry under strict conditions [PDF p. 63]. However, Roman officials, particularly Governor Lupicinus, engaged in extortion and withheld food supplies, driving the starving Goths to desperation [PDF p. 64]. A banquet incident at Marcianopolis triggered open rebellion, leading to a year of fierce fighting along the Balkans [PDF p. 64]. The author notes that while the Goths had adopted some civilization, their barbarian spirit remained potent [PDF p. 64]. In 378, Emperor Valens launched a major offensive against the Gothic forces near Adrianople [PDF p. 65]. The author highlights a critical shift in military tactics, noting that the Goths had adopted cavalry warfare, which contrasted sharply with traditional Roman infantry dominance [PDF p. 65]. During the battle, Gothic cavalry arrived unexpectedly and routed the Roman flanks [PDF p. 66]. The resulting crush of infantry led to a catastrophic defeat, killing forty thousand soldiers and the Emperor himself [PDF p. 67]. The author characterizes this as the most fearful defeat since Cannae, effectively destroying the Eastern Roman army [PDF p. 67]. Although the Goths advanced toward Constantinople, they abandoned the siege due to the city’s formidable walls [PDF p. 67]. The author concludes that this event validated Constantine’s earlier prescience regarding the capital’s defensive importance [PDF p. 67].

The author argues that Latin decayed in the East due to practical separation from the West and barbarian devastation [PDF p. 170]. By the seventh century, Latin knowledge was rare, with Justinian being the last emperor to speak it natively [PDF p. 169]. The author attributes this linguistic shift to the division of the empire and the extermination of Latin-speaking populations by Slavs [PDF p. 170]. Simultaneously, the empire became increasingly Christian [PDF p. 171]. The author notes that Christian influence on state machinery began slowly, accelerating under Theodosius I [PDF p. 171]. The author highlights that gladiatorial games ended after a monk’s death, not state decree [PDF p. 171]. Christianity also abolished infanticide and modified slavery by emphasizing the soul’s equality [PDF p. 173]. The author credits these social improvements to the Christian belief in individual worth [PDF p. 174]. However, the author explicitly evaluates the rise of monasticism as dangerous [PDF p. 174]. The author claims monks neglected civic duties, harming the state during barbarian invasions [PDF p. 175]. The author describes this apathy as maddening to pagans [PDF p. 176]. The author concludes that governing classes preserved Roman traditions despite this religious shift [PDF p. 176]. The author observes that paganism vanished, though indifference persisted among educated Christians [PDF p. 176]. The author suggests that while Christianity improved social conditions, its ascetic elements posed significant political risks to the empire’s stability [PDF p. 174].

The author characterizes the eighty years following Basil the Macedonian’s death as the most monotonous period in imperial history, dominated by the literary reigns of Leo VI and Constantine VII [PDF p. 241]. While these emperors were mild men of letters rather than military conquerors, the era experienced relative peace, with external threats limited to vexatious but non-dangerous piratical raids [PDF p. 242]. The author notes that the capture of Thessalonica by Saracens in 904 was a disgraceful administrative failure, though it occurred by surprise [PDF p. 242]. Constantine VII’s path to power was obstructed by regents, including his uncle Alexander and the ambitious admiral Romanus Lecapenus, until popular wrath removed the Lecapenus family, allowing Constantine to rule for twenty years [PDF p. 243]. The author evaluates their chief achievements as literary rather than political, highlighting Leo’s military manual as a valuable record of Byzantine organization and tactics [PDF p. 244]. This work reveals a highly disciplined army with specialized units and medical support, reflecting confidence in the empire’s defensive capabilities [PDF p. 245]. Constantine’s writings, particularly on court ceremonies, demonstrate his methodical nature and compensation for his lack of real power during his youth [PDF p. 247]. The author concludes that the literary output of these emperors signals the end of the intellectual dearth that had plagued Byzantium since the seventh century, marking a significant cultural revival [PDF p. 247].

The author argues that the Byzantine Empire ceased to be a vital bulwark for Christendom after 1370, asserting that its prolonged existence resulted from the Paleologi’s subservience to the Turks [PDF p. 358]. The text suggests that an earlier fall of Constantinople would have only marginally altered European history, potentially affecting Italian commerce and the timing of the Renaissance [PDF p. 359]. During the reign of John Paleologus, internal strife weakened the state, as his son Andronicus rebelled and was subsequently blinded [PDF p. 359]. John’s successor, Manuel II, lacked the resources for rebellion but capitalized on the Ottoman civil war triggered by Tamerlane’s victory in 1402 [PDF p. 360]. Manuel secured temporary territorial gains by selling his support to Turkish pretenders, yet the author notes that Europe missed a rare opportunity to expel the Ottomans due to Hungarian conflicts with the Hussites and poor relations with Serbia [PDF p. 362]. When Murad II unified the Ottoman realm, he reclaimed the territories Manuel had gained, forcing the Byzantines back into vassalage [PDF p. 363]. The author describes the subsequent decades as a period of unredeemed gloom, characterized by the physical decay of Constantinople and its economic dependence on Italian merchants [PDF p. 365]. John VI. maintained peace but lost Thessalonica to the Ottomans after his brother sold it to Venice [PDF p. 367]. Finally, John VIII. traveled to Italy to secure aid through religious union with Rome, but the author evaluates this effort as futile because the papacy was too weakened by internal schisms to provide meaningful military support [PDF p. 367].
